---
title: "Terminology and notation"
subtitle: "Targets, reporting losses and computation scope"
description: "Definitions of posterior quantities, common grades, multidomain profiles, disclosure, error measures and report families."
---

An Alabama county and a California school are both units, but their reports compare different outcomes. The
definitions below specify what is compared, how the posterior enters the comparison, and which reports can be chosen.

## Targets and posterior uncertainty

::: {.prx-glossary}

Unit; criterion $k$
:   A unit is a firm, school, site, or other entity included in the comparison. A criterion is an outcome or other target used to evaluate the report. For example, income and incarceration are two criteria measured for the same counties.

    **Examples:** [Multiple criteria](criteria/several-criteria.qmd) · [Supplied summaries](tools/your-data.qmd)

$\theta_i$
:   The target for unit $i$, coded so that higher values receive higher reporting priority. The application states what higher priority means for that target.

    **Examples:** [Two-unit comparison](uncertainty/two-units.qmd) · [Alabama counties](cases/alabama-map.qmd)

Posterior
:   The distribution of target values given the data and model. Posterior risk averages the loss over this distribution. Calibration concerns how those probabilities agree with outcomes under a specified evaluation law or in new data.

    **Examples:** [Posterior shrinkage](uncertainty/shrinkage.qmd) · [Posterior inputs](uncertainty/posterior-pipeline.qmd)

$\pi_{ij}$
:   The posterior probability of a direction such as $\Pr(\theta_i>\theta_j)$. This calculation uses the joint distribution of the two targets because the event depends on their difference.

    **Examples:** [Direction probabilities](uncertainty/two-units.qmd) · [Interval overlap](uncertainty/interval-overlap.qmd)

$e_{ij}^{(k)}$
:   The probability that stating $i$ above $j$ is wrong on criterion $k$. Under the zero-margin weak-error convention, equality makes either strict direction wrong. If equality has positive probability, the two directional errors sum to more than one. Each example specifies the event and any comparison margin.

    **Examples:** [Pairwise decisions](grades/one-pair.qmd) · [Posterior equality](grades/ties-and-withholding.qmd)

Marginal interval
:   An interval containing a specified share of the posterior distribution for one target. A 90% interval for each of two schools gives a probability statement about each school individually. The probability that one school's target exceeds the other's uses their joint posterior.

    **Example:** [Report-card summaries](grades/report-card.qmd)

Expected rank
:   The posterior average position of a unit under a specified rank and tie convention. Ordering these averages gives one possible ranking and can define a fixed-order report family.

    **Example:** [Alternative ranking summaries](uncertainty/which-ranking.qmd)

:::

## Grade reports, disclosure and error

::: {.prx-glossary}

Common-grade report $g$ (P1)
:   An ordered grouping of the units, with grade 1 at the high-priority end. The report states a direction between grades. Within a grade it leaves the comparison unstated. Using the report to allocate places or resources requires a separate rule.

    **Examples:** [Report construction](grades/report-builder.qmd) · [Allocation objectives](rules/one-place.qmd)

$n$, $M$
:   The number of included units and their $M=n(n-1)/2$ unordered pairs. Each cross-grade pair contributes one stated direction.

    **Example:** [Report-family counts](grades/how-many-reports.qmd)

$N$, $s=N/M$
:   The number of stated pairs and the disclosure share. The remaining $M-N$ pairs are withheld.

    **Example:** [Disclosure from tier sizes](rules/tier-sizes.qmd)

$E_k$
:   The posterior expected number of wrong stated directions on criterion $k$, obtained by summing directional error probabilities over the stated pairs. Joint correctness is a separate probability.

    **Example:** [Expected and realized errors](grades/disclosed-errors.qmd)

$E_k/N$
:   The expected wrong share among stated pairs of a fixed report. It is **NA: no disclosure** when $N=0$.

    **Example:** [Error-rate denominators](grades/two-denominators.qmd)

$DR_k=E_k/M$
:   The expected wrong count per possible pair. Withholding can reduce this rate by reducing the set of stated directions. The criterion subscript is usually omitted in single-criterion examples.

    **Example:** [Error-rate denominators](grades/two-denominators.qmd)

$\tau$
:   The cost per withheld pair when a wrong stated direction costs one. Weighted risk is $R_\tau=(E_w+\tau(M-N))/M$.

    **Example:** [Reporting risk](grades/price-of-silence.qmd)

$\lambda$, $\phi$
:   KRW's reward for a correct direction and the informed share in their stipulated audience model. The conversion is $\tau=\lambda/(1+\lambda)$ and $\phi=1-2\tau$. The positive-cost audience range is $0<\lambda\leq1$, $0<\tau\leq1/2$ and $0\leq\phi<1$. Equivalence of optimal reports requires the stated common-posterior, tie-free and common-family conditions.

    **Examples:** [Loss-scale conversion](cases/lambda-tau.qmd) · [Equivalent reporting losses](cases/krw-axes.qmd)

:::

A loss-minimizing report satisfies $E_w\leq\tau N$ when the family includes the report that withholds every
comparison. The inequality follows by comparing the chosen report's loss with that benchmark. A grade report
chosen by a different rule may exceed the benchmark.

## Report families and comparisons

::: {.prx-glossary}

Family; grade cap
:   The set of reports considered in the search. A grade cap limits the number of grades. A fixed order limits grade boundaries to cuts along that order, so the best report among those cuts may differ from the best report over all orders. Some fixed orders also keep equal scores together.

    **Examples:** [Report families](grades/families.qmd) · [Computation methods](grades/computing-grades.qmd)

Frontier
:   The lower convex boundary of expected wrong counts plotted against disclosure for a specified report family. A point on an edge may require randomizing between complete reports. Two reports can minimize risk at the same $\tau$ while stating different numbers of pairs.

    **Examples:** [Error–disclosure frontier](grades/frontier.qmd) · [Comparison constraints](rules/same-tau-or-same-n.qmd)

$\psi$
:   The probability of choosing the report that states more pairs in a mixture of two frontier reports. Expected disclosure averages the two pair counts using the mixing probabilities. An individual draw produces one of the two complete reports.

    **Example:** [Mixtures of reports](grades/frontier-mixtures.qmd)

$w_k$, $E_w=\sum_k w_k E_k$
:   Nonnegative criterion error weights summing to one, and the weighted expected wrong count. These weights apply to directional losses. Coefficients of a scalar composite target have a separate role.

    **Examples:** [Common grades](criteria/two-scores.qmd) · [Composite targets](criteria/composite-or-criterion.qmd)

$q_k$
:   An expected-error budget, expressed in count form as $E_k\leq q_kN$. With no stated directions both sides are zero, although the error share is undefined. Some applications use budgets only to evaluate the displayed report; others use them to restrict selection.

    **Examples:** [Budget-constrained families](criteria/error-budgets.qmd) · [Case-report checks](tools/report-designer.qmd)

$\Delta_k$
:   The risk of the common report on criterion $k$ minus the minimum risk for that criterion under the same loss and report family. If the exact minimum is unknown, bounds on it give an interval for the excess risk. Changing the loss or family changes the benchmark.

    **Example:** [Criterion-specific excess risk](criteria/common-grade-cost.qmd)

Selection belief; evaluation law
:   The distribution used to select a report and the distribution used to evaluate that fixed report. Using a different evaluation law can change expected loss for the same grade vector.

    **Examples:** [Alternative evaluation laws](grades/another-law.qmd) · [Selection-draw evaluation](grades/chosen-and-judged.qmd)

Joint correctness
:   The probability that all stated directions are correct together. Pairwise probabilities and expected wrong counts alone do not determine this event probability. Composite targets similarly require the relevant joint-law information.

    **Example:** [Limits of pairwise probabilities](criteria/pairs-leave-open.qmd)

Simulation error
:   Numerical uncertainty due to a finite set of posterior draws. Independent draws and dependent chains require different variance calculations and diagnostics. Increasing the number of draws reduces numerical error under the supplied law without establishing the adequacy of the model.

    **Examples:** [Independent-draw error](uncertainty/mc-error.qmd) · [Dependent-draw error](uncertainty/chain-draws.qmd)

:::

When repeated reports state different numbers of pairs, averaging their realized error fractions gives equal weight
to reports that state at least one pair. Dividing expected wrong counts by expected stated counts gives more weight to reports
that state more pairs. A posterior-reported share instead uses the probabilities supplied to that report.
[Averaging across reports](grades/averaging-errors.qmd) compares these quantities, and the
[case-report tool](tools/report-designer.qmd) specifies the denominator used in its report.

## Domain profiles and joint protection {#multidomain-profiles-and-joint-protection}

[Domain profiles](criteria/index.qmd#domain-profiles) give each unit a grade for each domain. The following
definitions explain how those grades are compared and how joint errors enter the choice of a report.

::: {.prx-glossary}

Domain $d$; profile matrix $G$
:   A substantive reporting coordinate and its grade column. The matrix has units on rows and domains on columns.
    A common-grade report uses the same column across criteria; a multidomain profile (P2) permits separate columns.
    Grade 1 denotes the highest reported priority within its own domain.

    **Example:** [Common grades and domain profiles](profiles/profile-common-vs-domain.qmd)

Profile tuple; crossed directions
:   A unit's ordered domain grades. Tuples such as $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ place the first unit higher in one domain and
    lower in the other. They do not define an overall ranking or an allocation rule. Equal grades within a domain
    withhold that pair's direction without asserting equal latent targets.

    **Examples:** [Common and profile reports](profiles/profile-common-vs-domain.qmd) · [Forty fictional sites](profiles/fictional-site-profiles.qmd)

Complete joint state
:   A set of target values for every included unit and domain in one posterior state. A complete finite law lists
    each possible state and its probability. Two laws can agree within each domain and differ in how the domains
    vary together. Row labels on separate simulations are insufficient to recover that dependence.

    **Example:** [Dependence and joint protection](profiles/profile-dependence.qmd)

$F_d$, $N_d$, $R(G)$
:   In a joint state, $F_d$ counts false strict directions in domain $d$; a strict assertion at latent equality is
    false. The reported card discloses $N_d$ pairs in that domain. Its additive expected loss is
    $R(G)=\sum_d w_d\{E(F_d)+\tau_d(M-N_d)\}/M$, with the original $M=n(n-1)/2$ pair count. This expected cost is
    distinct from a probability that one or more protected conditions fail.

    **Examples:** [Separate weighted choices](profiles/profile-separability.qmd) · [Reporting resolution](profiles/profile-resolution.qmd)

$t_d$, $\alpha$, $J(G)$
:   A strict false-direction-proportion threshold, an inclusive joint cap, and the direct union probability
    $J(G)=\Pr\{\text{at least one }d:\ F_d>t_dN_d\}$. The union is formed within the same joint state before its
    probability is calculated. At $N_d=0$ the ratio is not defined and the domain's exceedance event is false.
    Feasibility requires $J(G)\leq\alpha$, alongside any other declared constraints.

    **Example:** [Dependence and joint protection](profiles/profile-dependence.qmd)

Separable reporting decision
:   An additive weighted objective whose actual feasible family factors into a Cartesian product of domain
    choices. Every combination of the complete weighted domain minimizer sets is then optimal in that product.
    Posterior independence is unnecessary. A zero-weight domain contributes every feasible column to its weighted
    minimizer set, while retaining its constraints. A joint constraint can prevent the feasible family from factoring.

    **Example:** [When domain choices separate](profiles/profile-separability.qmd)

Occupied-grade counts $(K_S,K_C)$
:   The numbers of occupied grades in the two domains, rather than a particular site's profile tuple. With a fixed
    law, loss and candidate bank, relaxing a budget cannot increase minimum risk. A selected domain's grade count
    can nevertheless decrease as reporting detail moves to another domain. Count paths identify the canonical
    representative when there are tied optima.

    **Example:** [Posterior uncertainty and reporting resolution](profiles/profile-resolution.qmd)

Exact optimizer set; displayed representative
:   All feasible candidates that attain the same exact minimum loss. The app displays the first in a specified
    grade order and keeps the other tied reports available. The reported optimum is relative to the candidates
    included in the search.

    **Examples:** [Common versus separate columns](profiles/profile-common-vs-domain.qmd) · [Dependence and tied cards](profiles/profile-dependence.qmd)

Exact calculations for a finite law
:   For a complete list of posterior states and probabilities, the app computes losses and tests constraints with
    exact fractions. A separate assessment is required if the supplied law approximates another posterior. The
    browser examples accept 2–4 units, 1–2 domains, 1–8 states, and at most 256 distinct profile cards, with at most
    256 input columns per domain. The R package also supports assessment with independent draws and MCMC diagnostics.

    **Examples:** [Joint-law illustration](profiles/profile-dependence.qmd) · [Specified reversal scenarios](profiles/profile-resolution.qmd)

Saved profiles for fictional sites
:   The forty-site example shows grade tuples, the settings used to choose them, and separate summaries for
    selection and diagnostics. The grade tuples identify occupied cells and the directions stated in each
    domain. Rerunning selection or computing new risk probabilities would require the original joint draws.
    The stored fractions describe the draws used. The diagnostic segment came from the same chain as the
    selection segment, so it does not provide an independent validation.

    **Example:** [Profiles of forty fictional sites](profiles/fictional-site-profiles.qmd)

:::
